name: Abraham

seo.title: Abraham: his life, the binding of Isaac and how he died
seo.description: Abraham in plain words: the call from Ur, the covenant under the stars, the three visitors, the binding of Isaac, his feast days, and the myths.

band.lede: The herdsman God called out of Ur. He believed the promise of a son and a land, and became the father of many nations.

who: Abraham was a herdsman from Ur, in Mesopotamia. God called him to leave his home for a land He would show him, and promised to make him a great nation. At seventy-five he went, still childless. At a hundred, he and Sarah had Isaac, the son God had promised. Jews, Christians and Muslims all honour him.

tidbits.text: He is the first person the Bible calls a prophet. God tells King Abimelech, “he is a prophet; he will pray for you.” He is the first it calls a Hebrew, too.

cite.text: Genesis 20:7; 14:13; Strong's Hebrew 5030 and 5680, at Bible Hub

tidbits.text: The Bible calls him God's friend three times: in a king's prayer, “Abraham Your friend”, in Isaiah, and in James.
Moriah, where he took Isaac, is named only once more in the Bible. Solomon built the temple “in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah”.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In **Ur of the Chaldeans**, in Mesopotamia, in a year no one recorded. Most scholars take it to be the Sumerian city of **Ur**, in southern Iraq, says *Britannica*. The OCA dates his life to about **2000 BC**.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: A **tent**. He moved from **Haran** to **Shechem** and **Bethel**, to the **Oaks of Mamre** at **Hebron**, and to **Beersheba**.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His father was **Terah**, and his brothers were **Nahor** and **Haran**. His wife **Sarah** was his half-sister. His sons were **Ishmael** by Hagar and **Isaac** by Sarah, and six more by **Keturah**. **Lot** was his nephew.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **herdsman**, “extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold”.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Abram**, until he was 99. **The Hebrew**. **God's friend**. **The father of all who believe**, in Paul's words. The **Forefather**, in the Orthodox Church.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: In the **cave of Machpelah**, near Mamre at **Hebron**, beside Sarah. It was the field he had bought for her grave.

facts.label: Honoured by
facts.text: **Jews**, **Christians** and **Muslims**, says *Britannica*. Jews and Christians trace God's promise through **Isaac**. In Islam it passes through **Ishmael**, and Muhammad is his descendant.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: At his tent, serving **three visitors**. Or on the mountain with Isaac, as an **angel** stops his hand. The Orthodox icon of the three visitors is the *Hospitality of Abraham*.

portrait.alt: A painting by Guercino: Abraham, an old man with a white beard, a blue turban and a blue cloak over a red robe, raises one hand and points away with the other. Hagar, in a white blouse, turns to look back at him with tears in her eyes, and the boy Ishmael weeps into his hands beside her. On the left, Sarah stands with her back turned.

feasts.note: The Orthodox also keep him on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers, between 11 and 17 December, and on the Sunday before Christmas with all the forefathers of Christ. Churches on the old calendar keep 9 October 13 days later, on 22 October.

quotes.q: Abraham, styled ‘the friend,’ was found faithful, inasmuch as he rendered obedience to the words of God.

moments.title: Out of Ur
moments.text: Abram grew up in Ur of the Chaldeans, the son of Terah. His brother Haran died there, leaving a son, Lot. Abram's wife Sarai “was barren; she had no children.” Terah set out with Abram, Sarai and Lot for the land of Canaan. “But when they arrived in Haran, they settled there.” Terah died in Haran. Joshua later said Terah and his fathers had “worshiped other gods.” Stephen, in Acts, says God first appeared to Abraham “while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran”.

moments.title: “Go to the land I will show you”
moments.text: The LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father's household, and go to the land I will show you.” He promised to make him a great nation, and more: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” “So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him.” He was seventy-five. He took Sarai, Lot and all they had into Canaan. At Shechem the LORD appeared to him: “I will give this land to your offspring.” Abram built an altar there. Hebrews says he went “without knowing where he was going.”

moments.title: “Say you are my sister”
moments.text: Famine drove Abram down to Egypt. At the border he said to Sarai, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman.” He was afraid the Egyptians would kill him to take her. “Please say you are my sister.” Pharaoh took her into his palace, and treated Abram well for her sake. Then the LORD struck Pharaoh's household with plagues. Pharaoh summoned Abram: “What have you done to me? Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?” He sent them away with all they had. Years later, at Gerar, Abraham did the same again.

moments.title: Parting from Lot
moments.text: Abram came back from Egypt “extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold.” Lot had flocks and herds too, and their herdsmen quarrelled. Abram let his nephew choose first. “Is not the whole land before you? Now separate yourself from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right.” Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan, and pitched his tent toward Sodom. Then the LORD told Abram to look north, south, east and west: “for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever.” Abram moved his tent to the Oaks of Mamre, at Hebron.

moments.title: The rescue, and Melchizedek
moments.text: Four kings raided the cities of the plain and carried off Lot. Abram “mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household.” He chased the raiders as far as Dan, attacked by night, and brought back Lot, the people and the goods. On his way home Melchizedek, king of Salem, came out to meet him with bread and wine. He was “priest of God Most High”, and he blessed Abram. Abram gave him a tenth of everything. The king of Sodom offered him the spoils, but Abram would not take so much as a thread.

moments.title: Count the stars
moments.text: The word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.” Abram answered that he had no child. His heir would be a servant, Eliezer of Damascus. The LORD took him outside. “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then He told him, “So shall your offspring be.” And “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”

moments.title: The smoking firepot
moments.text: Abram asked, “Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?” The LORD told him to bring a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon. Abram split the animals and laid the halves opposite each other, and drove the birds of prey away. As the sun set, “great terror and darkness overwhelmed him.” God told him his descendants would be strangers and slaves for four hundred years, and then come back. After dark, “a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves”. That day the LORD made a covenant with Abram.

moments.place: A spring on the road to Shur
moments.title: Hagar
moments.text: Sarai was still childless. She gave Abram her Egyptian servant Hagar: “perhaps I can build a family by her.” Hagar conceived, and began to despise her mistress. Sarai treated her so harshly that she fled. The angel of the LORD found her by a spring in the desert and sent her back with a promise. Her son would be called Ishmael, “for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.” Hagar gave the LORD a name: “You are the God who sees me.” Abram was eighty-six when Ishmael was born.

moments.title: A new name
moments.text: The LORD appeared to Abram again. “I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless.” Then: “No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.” Sarai would be Sarah, and she would bear him a son. Abraham fell facedown and laughed. “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” He pleaded for the son he had: “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” God promised to bless Ishmael, but the covenant would pass through Isaac. That same day Abraham, Ishmael and every male in his household were circumcised.

moments.when: In the heat of the day
moments.title: Three visitors
moments.text: “The LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent.” He looked up and saw three men. He ran to meet them and bowed low. “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree.” He hurried to Sarah for fresh bread, ran to the herd for a choice calf, and brought curds and milk. He stood by them under the tree while they ate. Then the LORD said Sarah would have a son within a year. Listening at the tent door, she laughed to herself. “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?”

moments.title: The plea for Sodom
moments.text: The LORD told Abraham of the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah. Abraham stepped forward. “Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?” He asked for the city to be spared for fifty righteous people. Then for forty-five, and forty, and thirty, and twenty. “May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak once more. Suppose ten are found there?” The answer came: “On account of the ten, I will not destroy it.” Early next morning he looked down toward Sodom and saw the smoke rising “like smoke from a furnace.” But God “remembered Abraham”, and brought Lot out.

moments.title: Isaac
moments.text: “The LORD did for Sarah what He had promised.” She bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the very time God had said, and he named him Isaac. Abraham was a hundred years old. Sarah said, “God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.” When the boy was weaned, Abraham held a great feast.

moments.title: Hagar and Ishmael sent away
moments.text: At the feast, Sarah saw Hagar's son mocking Isaac. “Expel the slave woman and her son,” she told Abraham. “Now this matter distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son Ishmael.” God told him to listen to Sarah, and promised to make a nation of Ishmael too. Early in the morning Abraham put bread and a skin of water on Hagar's shoulders, and sent her away with the boy. When the water ran out in the desert, she sat down a bowshot away and wept. God heard the boy's voice, and opened her eyes to a well. “And God was with the boy.”

moments.title: The binding of Isaac
moments.text: “Some time later God tested Abraham.” He said, “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering.” Abraham got up early, saddled his donkey, split the wood and set out. On the third day he saw the place in the distance. He told his servants, “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.” On the way up, Isaac carried the wood and asked where the lamb was. Abraham built the altar, bound his son, laid him on the wood and took the knife. The angel of the LORD called from heaven, “Abraham, Abraham!” “Do not lay a hand on the boy.” Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket, and offered it in his son's place. He named the place The LORD Will Provide. Hebrews says he “reasoned that God could raise the dead”.

moments.title: A grave for Sarah
moments.text: Sarah died at Hebron, aged 127, “and Abraham went out to mourn and to weep for her.” He owned no land. He said to the Hittites of the town, “I am a foreigner and an outsider among you.” He asked to buy the cave of Machpelah from Ephron. Ephron offered it as a gift, then named its worth: “four hundred shekels of silver, but what is that between you and me?” Abraham weighed out the full price in front of them all, and buried Sarah there.

moments.title: A wife for Isaac
moments.text: Abraham was old, and “the LORD had blessed him in every way.” He made his chief servant swear to find Isaac a wife from his own kindred, not from the Canaanites. Isaac must never be taken back to the old country. “The LORD, the God of heaven, who brought me from my father's house and my native land ... He will send His angel before you.” The servant went, and came back with Rebekah. “And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother's death.”

words.note: He wrote nothing. Genesis records what he said, to God and to others. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.kicker: On the way up the mountain
feature.q: God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.
feature.ctx: Isaac had asked him, “The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” The two walked on together.

quotes.q: Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are kinsmen.
quotes.who: To Lot, when their herdsmen quarrelled over the land.

quotes.q: I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, that I will not accept even a thread, or a strap of a sandal, or anything that belongs to you, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’
quotes.who: To the king of Sodom, who offered him the spoils of the battle.

quotes.q: O Lord GOD, what can You give me, since I remain childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?
quotes.who: His first words to God that Genesis records, after the promise of a “very great reward”.

quotes.q: Far be it from You! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?
Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord—though I am but dust and ashes—suppose the fifty righteous ones lack five. Will You destroy the whole city for the lack of five?
quotes.who: Pleading for Sodom, a second time.

myths.claim: Abraham smashed the idols in his father's shop.
myths.truth: Not in the Bible. It says only that Terah, his father, “worshiped other gods.” The shop is a later Jewish legend, told in the midrash *Genesis Rabbah*. There a man comes to buy an idol, and Abraham asks his age. Seventy, says the man. Abraham answers, “how canst thou adore a god so much younger than thou?” An older book, *Jubilees*, from the second century BC, has him set fire to the house of idols.

myths.claim: Isaac was a little boy on the mountain.
myths.truth: Genesis never gives his age. It calls him “the boy”, and he was old enough to carry the wood up the mountain. Josephus, writing about 93, says, “Isaac was twenty-five years old.” Clement of Rome says Isaac “cheerfully yielded himself as a sacrifice.”

cite.text: Genesis 22:5-6; Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 13; 1 Clement, chapter 31

myths.truth: Genesis says “the LORD appeared to Abraham”, and he saw three men. Two of them went on to Sodom, and Genesis then calls them “the two angels”. Abraham “remained standing before the LORD.” Justin Martyr, about 155, read the One Who stayed as God, “sent with the two angels in His company”. Orthodox icons of the scene paint all three as angels at his table. Andrei Rublev's icon of them, painted in the 1400s, is known simply as the *Trinity*.

cite.text: Genesis 18:1-22; 19:1; Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 56

myths.claim: When he said Sarah was his sister, it was simply a lie.
myths.truth: By his own account it was half true: “she really is my sister, the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother—and she became my wife.” But he said it to hide that she was his wife, because he was afraid: “They will kill me on account of my wife.” He did it twice, and both kings rebuked him. Pharaoh asked, “What have you done to me?”

extras.title: Faith and works
extras.lede: Paul and James both quote the same verse about him: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” Paul uses it to show that God counts faith as righteousness, apart from works. James sets it beside the day Abraham offered Isaac, to show that faith must act. Christians have long read the two together. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: Paul, in Romans
items.text: Paul points out that God counted Abraham righteous before he was circumcised. So Abraham is “the father of all who believe”, Jew or Gentile.
items.quote: However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.

items.title: James, in his letter
items.text: James asks what good faith is if it does nothing. He points to the day Abraham offered Isaac on the altar, and draws his lesson: “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.”
items.quote: You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did.

items.title: The Catholic reading
items.text: The Council of Trent, in 1547, taught that nothing before justification, “whether faith or works”, earns it. It is given freely. Once justified, believers grow in it, “faith co-operating with good works”, and here Trent quotes James. Of faith it said:
items.quote: we are therefore said to be justified by faith, because faith is the beginning of human salvation, the foundation, and the root of all Justification

cite.text: Council of Trent, Decree on Justification, chapters 8 and 10, in Philip Schaff's The Creeds of Christendom

items.title: A Protestant reading
items.text: The Westminster Confession of 1646, the standard of Presbyterian churches, answers James this way. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone:
items.quote: Faith, thus receiving and resting on Christ and His righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification; yet is it not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love.

cite.text: The Westminster Confession, chapter 11, in Philip Schaff's The Creeds of Christendom

items.title: The Orthodox reading
items.text: The *Longer Catechism* of Philaret of Moscow, approved by the Russian Church's Holy Synod, asks whether faith alone is enough for a Christian, without love and good works. It answers:
items.quote: No; for faith without love and good works is inactive and dead, and so can not lead to eternal life.

cite.text: The Longer Catechism, question 482, tr. R. W. Blackmore, in Philip Schaff's The Creeds of Christendom

circle.name: Sarah
circle.text: His wife, and his half-sister, the daughter of his father by another mother. She was barren for most of her life. At ninety she laughed at the promise of a son, and then bore Isaac. She died at 127, and he wept for her. Isaiah says, “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth.”

circle.name: Isaac
circle.text: The son of the promise, born when Abraham was a hundred. He carried the wood up Mount Moriah. He married Rebekah, and “was comforted after his mother's death.” With Ishmael, he buried his father.

circle.name: Ishmael
circle.text: His firstborn, by Hagar, born when Abraham was 86. When Sarah wanted him gone, “this matter distressed Abraham greatly”. God promised to make him a great nation too, and he grew up in the wilderness and “became a great archer.”

circle.name: Hagar
circle.text: Sarah's Egyptian servant, who bore him Ishmael. Twice she ended up in the desert, and twice God met her there. She gave the LORD a name of her own: “You are the God who sees me.”

circle.name: Lot
circle.text: His nephew, the son of his dead brother Haran. He came with Abraham from Haran, then chose the green plain of the Jordan and settled near Sodom. Abraham rescued him from four kings and pleaded for Sodom. Peter's second letter calls him “a righteous man”. The Orthodox remember them together on 9 October.

circle.name: Melchizedek
circle.text: King of Salem, and “priest of God Most High”. He met Abraham after the battle with bread and wine, and blessed him. Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. Hebrews calls him “like the Son of God”, a priest for all time.

circle.name: Terah
circle.text: His father, who “worshiped other gods”, says Joshua. He led the family out of Ur toward Canaan, but they stopped at Haran, and he died there at 205.

circle.name: Abimelech
circle.text: The king of Gerar. He took Sarah, believing she was Abraham's sister, until God warned him in a dream. Later he came to make peace: “God is with you in all that you do.” The two swore an oath at Beersheba.

circle.name: His chief servant
circle.text: “The chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned.” He swore to find Isaac a wife in the land Abraham had come from, and brought back Rebekah. Genesis never names him. Earlier, Abraham had named his heir as Eliezer of Damascus.

circle.name: Keturah
circle.text: The wife he took later in life. She bore him six sons, Midian among them. He gave them gifts and sent them east, away from Isaac.

death.big: He died at 175, “old and contented”. Isaac and Ishmael buried him beside Sarah, in the cave of Machpelah.
paras: God had told him long before, “You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age.”

Before he died, he left everything he owned to Isaac. He gave gifts to the sons of his other wives, and sent them away to the east. “And at a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and contented, and was gathered to his people.”

“His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre.” It was the field he had bought for Sarah's grave. Stephen says God gave him “not even a foot of ground” in Canaan as an inheritance, only the promise.
Josephus, writing about 93, closes his story: “He was a man of incomparable virtue, and honored by God in a manner agreeable to his piety towards him.”

Hebrews says of him and his family that they “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar.” Jesus spoke of him as alive to God. God is “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, and “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”

later.title: What Josephus saw at Hebron
later.text: In the 70s, Josephus wrote that the family's tombs were still shown at Hebron: “the fabric of which monuments are of the most excellent marble, and wrought after the most elegant manner.” Six furlongs from the town stood “a very large turpentine tree”. People said it had stood there since the creation of the world.

cite.text: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews, book 4, chapter 9, tr. William Whiston

saint.big: Yes. He is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic calendars, on 9 October.

churches.note: Not in the English or Episcopal calendars

paras: The Orthodox call him the Forefather. The OCA keeps his day on 9 October, with his nephew Lot. He is honoured again on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers, two Sundays before Christmas. It remembers the ancestors of Christ, “especially the Patriarch Abraham”.
There is no Mass for him in the Roman calendar. But the Litany of the Saints, in the form Rome published in 1969, calls on him by name, first among the patriarchs and prophets.

The Coptic Church keeps him on one day with Isaac and Jacob. Its synaxarium asks, “Who can describe the virtues of he who became father to many nations?” The Missouri Synod's calendar remembers him on 9 October as Abraham, Patriarch.
Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, gives his day like this:

quotes.q: The same day, the commemoration of the holy patriarch Abraham, father of all believers.

kin.name: Ruth
kin.text: Like him, she left her own land for a people she did not know. Boaz praised her for how she “left your father and mother and the land of your birth”.

kin.name: Rahab
kin.text: James names her straight after Abraham, as one whose faith showed in what she did: she “welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route”.

kin.name: Martha
kin.text: She “welcomed Him into her home”, and was soon busy with all the serving, as Abraham hurried to feed his three guests.
